Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective clinical-validity and discordance study•October 1, 2026

Clinical context helps explain definite-zone p-tau217 discordance

Among 706 Mayo Clinic patients with plasma p-tau217 outside the intermediate zone and confirmatory amyloid PET and/or CSF, 60 (8.5%) were discordant: false negatives were more common than false positives (5.6% vs 2.8%; p=0.007), with disease stage, kidney function, body mass index and obstructive sleep apnea associated with discordance patterns.

Key quantitative results: Sixty of 706 patients (8.5%) had discordant results. False negatives occurred in 5.6% and false positives in 2.8% (p=0.007). Across both discordance types, older age was associated with discordance (OR 1.61 per decade; 95% CI 1.23–2.14), as was obstructive sleep apnea (OR 1.94; 95% CI 1.08–3.49).

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217AmyloidBiological confirmation

Added October 2, 2026 · DOI:10.1212/WNL.0000000000218591; PMID:42821845

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Definite-zone p-tau217 results agreed with established amyloid measures in most patients, but discordance was not random. False negatives clustered with milder clinical stage, higher body mass index, better kidney function and obstructive sleep apnea; false positives clustered with older age, lower kidney function and more advanced impairment. These are signals for confirmatory testing and contextual interpretation, not post hoc permission to relabel a discordant result or use the associations as correction factors.

Study design

Investigators retrospectively identified 706 Mayo Clinic patients whose plasma p-tau217 was definitely positive (>0.324 pg/mL) or definitely negative (<0.186 pg/mL) and who had an amyloid PET and/or CSF p-tau181/Aβ42 result. They classified plasma results as true positive, true negative, false positive or false negative against the established biomarker result and modeled demographic, clinical, comorbidity and laboratory factors associated with discordance.

Key quantitative results

  • Sixty of 706 patients (8.5%) had discordant results. False negatives occurred in 5.6% and false positives in 2.8% (p=0.007). Across both discordance types, older age was associated with discordance (OR 1.61 per decade; 95% CI 1.23–2.14), as was obstructive sleep apnea (OR 1.94; 95% CI 1.08–3.49).
  • Compared with true positives, false negatives had higher MMSE scores (OR 1.20 per point), more obstructive sleep apnea (OR 2.01), higher body mass index (OR 1.11 per kg/m²) and higher estimated glomerular filtration rate (OR 1.33 per 10 mL/min/1.73 m²). Age-adjusted analyses retained body mass index (OR 1.14), estimated glomerular filtration rate (OR 1.63) and earlier Clinical Dementia Rating stage as associations.
  • Compared with true negatives, false positives were associated with older age (OR 2.37 per decade), thyroid disease (OR 4.41), lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (OR 0.48 per 10 mL/min/1.73 m²) and more advanced Clinical Dementia Rating stage. In age-adjusted analyses, estimated glomerular filtration rate remained associated (OR 0.54), while CDR ≥1 carried OR 11.11 versus CDR 0 and OR 4.55 versus CDR 0.5.

What changed

An October 1 Neurology report quantifies the residual discordance within definite plasma p-tau217 zones and identifies clinical patterns that can guide when a seemingly definitive result still warrants adjudication with PET, CSF or broader diagnostic evaluation.

Strength of evidence

Moderate clinical-validity and interpretation evidence from a 706-patient specialty-center cohort with established-biomarker comparators. Associations are observational, several subgroups are small, the reference standard combines PET and CSF, and the public abstract does not establish prospective decision impact or transportability to other assays and settings.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A definite plasma result should be interpreted alongside clinical stage and kidney function, with attention to obesity and obstructive sleep apnea when the phenotype and biomarker disagree. The findings support targeted confirmation rather than automatic acceptance or mathematical adjustment of the plasma value.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to blood-biomarker triage, discordant-result workups, specialty referral, pretest counseling and communication about why two-cutoff algorithms reduce but do not eliminate uncertainty.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The study used an assay-specific two-cutoff plasma p-tau217 workflow, with definite negative below 0.186 pg/mL and definite positive above 0.324 pg/mL. The public abstract does not name the assay platform; the cutoffs and associations should not be transferred to other products, matrices or workflows without validation.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, availability, guideline or coverage change occurred. The study may improve selection for confirmatory testing, but payer requirements and product-specific intended uses remain unchanged.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does 8.5% mean the test was only 91.5% accurate?
Not necessarily. The cohort included only definite-zone plasma results with PET and/or CSF confirmation, and the analysis focused on discordance rather than a population-screening accuracy estimate. Prevalence, referral patterns and the combined reference standard affect the observed proportion.
Should kidney function or body mass index be used to correct p-tau217 values?
No correction equation was validated. These variables identify contexts in which discordance was more likely and may justify confirmation; they do not establish a new adjusted cutoff.
Did the study establish clinical utility?
No. It supports clinical validity and contextual interpretation but did not test whether using these factors improves decisions, treatment eligibility, outcomes, safety or cost.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective specialty-center cohort
  • Observational associations cannot establish why discordance occurred
  • Amyloid PET and CSF p-tau181/Aβ42 were combined as the established-biomarker reference
  • Only 60 discordant cases, with smaller false-positive and false-negative subgroups
  • Public abstract does not name the assay platform or report external validation
  • No prospective decision-impact, treatment-access or patient-outcome evaluation

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Shir D, Algeciras-Schimnich A, Piura YD, et al. Clinical factors associated with discordant plasma P-Tau217 and established Alzheimer disease biomarkers. Neurology. Published online October 1, 2026. doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000218591.

Practice-relevant•Proposed Medicare Local Coverage Determination and evidence review•October 1, 2026

Noridian proposes noncoverage for AI brain-MRI quantification

A Noridian proposed Local Coverage Determination would make AI tools that automatically detect or quantify brain-MRI findings—including ARIA and volumetry—noncovered across its Medicare jurisdictions because the contractor found insufficient evidence of clinical utility; the proposal is not final, with comments open October 1–November 14, 2026.

Key label details: The proposed determination states that AI assistive tools for automated detection and/or quantification of brain-MRI findings are not reasonable and necessary and therefore would not be covered if the LCD is finalized as written.

ManagementMRIARIA monitoring

Added October 2, 2026 · CMS Proposed LCD DL40454; MCD LCD ID 40453, version 5

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The draft draws a sharp line between regulatory clearance and covered clinical utility. Noridian concludes that automated brain-MRI detection and quantification tools have not shown that their measurements improve diagnosis, monitoring, management or outcomes beyond clinician interpretation. If finalized as written, the noncoverage position would apply broadly across Noridian jurisdictions and could affect AI-assisted ARIA workflows as anti-amyloid treatment scales. It remains open to evidence and public comment.

Study design

Noridian reviewed published evidence, professional guidance and regulatory information for AI software that assists with automated detection and/or quantification of brain-MRI findings. The proposed LCD applies the Medicare reasonable-and-necessary standard and discusses ARIA software and volumetric or neurodegeneration products. It proposes noncoverage rather than issuing a clinical-practice recommendation.

Key label details

  • The proposed determination states that AI assistive tools for automated detection and/or quantification of brain-MRI findings are not reasonable and necessary and therefore would not be covered if the LCD is finalized as written.
  • The evidence review found no randomized trials showing improved patient outcomes, no professional guideline recommending routine use for the covered question and insufficient evidence that automated measurements change diagnosis, treatment decisions or monitoring compared with clinician interpretation.
  • The draft was posted October 1, 2026, with comments accepted through November 14 and an open meeting on October 22. It covers Noridian Medicare jurisdictions, including multiple western states and U.S. Pacific territories, but has no current effective date because it is still proposed.

What changed

A Medicare Administrative Contractor has opened formal consideration of a broad noncoverage policy for AI-assisted brain-MRI quantification, including tools used in ARIA monitoring, creating a material but not-yet-effective access signal.

Strength of evidence

The policy status is authoritative for a proposed Noridian coverage action, while the underlying clinical-utility conclusion reflects a contractor evidence review rather than new comparative trial data. The record explicitly identifies evidence gaps, and the conclusion may change after public comment.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Clinicians still must perform label-directed MRI monitoring and expert interpretation for anti-amyloid therapy. The proposal concerns reimbursement for adjunctive AI analysis, not whether MRI itself is necessary or covered, and it should not be treated as a final denial until Noridian completes the LCD process.

Field medical relevance

Important for imaging services, infusion programs, ARIA-monitoring workflows, vendors and medical-affairs teams separating FDA clearance, clinical availability, guideline endorsement and Medicare coverage.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The draft addresses software that assists clinicians by automatically detecting or quantifying brain-MRI abnormalities, including ARIA-focused and neurodegeneration/volumetry products. It is a coverage proposal, not a finding that the underlying MRI findings lack clinical relevance.

Access or reimbursement relevance

High but prospective. If finalized, the draft would establish noncoverage for automated brain-MRI detection and quantification tools in Noridian jurisdictions; it presently creates a comment opportunity and signals the evidence expected for future coverage rather than changing payment today.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is Medicare already refusing payment for these tools?
This document is a proposed LCD, not a final effective policy. Current claims remain subject to existing rules while the comment and finalization process proceeds.
Does the proposal eliminate MRI monitoring for Leqembi or Kisunla?
No. It addresses reimbursement for adjunctive AI detection or quantification software. It does not remove label-directed MRI monitoring or the need for qualified clinical interpretation.
Is FDA clearance enough for Medicare coverage?
No. FDA authorization and Medicare coverage answer different questions. Noridian acknowledges authorized products but says the record does not yet establish reasonable-and-necessary clinical utility for payment.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Proposed, not final or effective
  • Applies to Noridian jurisdictions rather than all Medicare contractors
  • Broad technology category contains products with different functions and evidence bases
  • Evidence review found little direct comparative or outcomes research
  • Final language may change after the comment period
  • Does not determine coverage of the underlying MRI examination or anti-amyloid drug

Primary source

Noridian Healthcare Solutions. Proposed LCD DL40454: Artificial Intelligence Assistive Tools for Automated Detection and Quantification of Brain MRI Findings. Posted October 1, 2026.

Practice-relevant•Private-payer medical policy update bulletin•October 1, 2026

UMR revises anti-amyloid coverage criteria for November

An October 1 UMR policy bulletin sets November 1 coverage criteria that align Leqembi and Kisunla with updated MRI/ARIA monitoring, require specialist oversight and biomarker-confirmed early Alzheimer disease, and add maintenance rules—including Kisunla amyloid-PET reassessment and Leqembi dosing expectations after 18 months.

Key label details: For Kisunla, initial coverage requires mild cognitive impairment or mild Alzheimer dementia, positive amyloid PET, a baseline brain MRI within 12 months, no concurrent anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody and label-consistent dosing. The policy lists MMSE 20–30, MoCA 17–30 or SLUMS 17–30 in its medically necessary pathway and specifies MRI monitoring before the second, third, fourth and seventh infusions, with additional imaging as clinically indicated.

ManagementAmyloid PETDisease-modifying treatment eligibility

Added October 2, 2026 · UMR Medical Policy Update Bulletin, October 2026; effective 2026-11-01

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The update operationalizes eligibility, safety monitoring and long-term treatment rules rather than merely repeating drug labels. Both policies require MCI or mild dementia due to Alzheimer disease, confirmed amyloid, recent baseline MRI and specialist oversight. The details differ: Kisunla coverage uses amyloid PET and adds ongoing PET-based continuation requirements; Leqembi allows specified CSF ratios or PET and defines expectations for monthly IV maintenance after 18 months while recognizing the self-administered subcutaneous product under the pharmacy benefit.

Study design

UMR's October 2026 Medical Policy Update Bulletin summarizes revised Leqembi and Kisunla medical-benefit coverage templates for UnitedHealthcare commercial and individual-exchange benefit plans. The policies specify initial and continuation criteria, biomarker confirmation, cognitive-stage thresholds, MRI schedules, counseling, specialist involvement, dosing and authorization duration. This is an access-policy action, not a clinical study or formal guideline.

Key label details

  • For Kisunla, initial coverage requires mild cognitive impairment or mild Alzheimer dementia, positive amyloid PET, a baseline brain MRI within 12 months, no concurrent anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody and label-consistent dosing. The policy lists MMSE 20–30, MoCA 17–30 or SLUMS 17–30 in its medically necessary pathway and specifies MRI monitoring before the second, third, fourth and seventh infusions, with additional imaging as clinically indicated.
  • Kisunla continuation authorizations remain 12 months. Through 18 months, a positive baseline amyloid PET or a plan to obtain one by month 18 is required; after 18 months, the policy calls for at least annual post-treatment amyloid PET that remains positive, along with continued ARIA monitoring, specialist oversight and no other anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody.
  • For Leqembi, amyloid confirmation may use PET or specified CSF ratios. The policy recognizes IQLIK under the pharmacy benefit, and for intravenous maintenance after 18 months expects every-four-week dosing; continued every-two-week dosing requires prescriber attestation that transition is not clinically appropriate. Continuation MRI monitoring is listed after one, two, three and six months and as clinically indicated.

What changed

An October 1 payer bulletin announces November 1 operational coverage rules for updated anti-amyloid dosing, MRI safety monitoring, biomarker confirmation and continuation, including new distinctions between Leqembi formulations and maintenance schedules.

Strength of evidence

Authoritative evidence of the named payer's published policy change and effective date. The bulletin does not grade underlying clinical evidence, test outcomes or establish that these criteria are optimal; applicability depends on the member's specific plan and benefit administration.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Infusion and memory-clinic teams may need to adjust prior-authorization packets, MRI timing, biomarker documentation and long-term treatment plans before November 1. Label-compliant care does not by itself guarantee coverage when a plan imposes additional documentation or continuation requirements.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to anti-amyloid treatment access, patient counseling, prior authorization, specialty-pharmacy routing, ARIA monitoring and the distinction among FDA labeling, clinical guidance and payer coverage.

Access or reimbursement relevance

High. The update directly changes documentation, monitoring and continuation criteria for covered anti-amyloid therapy in affected plans, while leaving authorization, general availability and other payer policies unchanged.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Are these national Medicare criteria?
No. This is a UMR/UnitedHealthcare private-plan policy update. Medicare and other payers may use different rules, and the member's specific benefit plan controls.
Does the policy take effect immediately?
No. The bulletin was published October 1, 2026, and lists November 1, 2026, as the effective date for the identified policy changes.
Is the Kisunla annual amyloid PET requirement an FDA recommendation?
It is a payer continuation criterion described in this policy. Payer coverage criteria, FDA labeling and clinical-practice recommendations should be documented separately.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Policy applies only to identified UMR/UnitedHealthcare plan contexts
  • Benefit documents and member-specific plan terms supersede a general bulletin
  • Criteria become effective November 1 rather than on the October 1 publication date
  • Bulletin summarizes policy language and does not grade the clinical evidence base
  • Coverage approval does not establish comparative effectiveness or clinical utility
  • Other payers may use different biomarker, MRI, dosing and continuation requirements

Primary source

UMR. Medical Policy Update Bulletin: October 2026. Leqembi and Kisunla policy updates effective November 1, 2026. Published October 1, 2026.

Early signal•Peer-reviewed prospective interventional pilot trial•September 29, 2026

Twenty-person ultrasound pilot supports feasibility, not efficacy

In a single-arm pilot of 20 amyloid-PET-positive patients with prodromal or mild Alzheimer disease, four weeks of low-intensity ultrasound caused no severe adverse events or MRI-detected hemorrhage, microbleeding or edema; executive-test and NPI scores improved, but MMSE, attention and quality of life did not, and the uncontrolled design precludes efficacy claims.

Key quantitative results: No severe adverse events occurred, and post-treatment MRI showed no intracerebral hemorrhage, microbleeding or brain edema in the 20 treated participants.

Clinical TrialsExperimental treatment safety

Added September 30, 2026 · DOI:10.1177/13872877261493067; PMID:42808496

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The trial establishes that a repeated four-week bilateral frontal and temporal ultrasound protocol was feasible in a very small biomarker-confirmed early-AD group, without the MRI safety signals reported in the abstract. Nominal improvements in Trail Making and neuropsychiatric scores are hypothesis-generating only: there was no sham arm, the sample was 20, several outcomes were tested, and global cognition, attention and quality of life did not significantly change.

Study design

Twenty people with amyloid-PET-positive prodromal Alzheimer disease or mild Alzheimer dementia received low-intensity ultrasound targeting bilateral frontal and temporal regions three times weekly for four weeks. Neurological examinations and brain MRI assessed safety. Exploratory outcomes included Trail Making Test-Black & White parts A and B, Attention Questionnaire Scale, Korean Quality of Life, MMSE and Neuropsychiatric Inventory; resting-state functional MRI was analyzed in a subset.

Key quantitative results

  • No severe adverse events occurred, and post-treatment MRI showed no intracerebral hemorrhage, microbleeding or brain edema in the 20 treated participants.
  • Trail Making Test-Black & White part A decreased from 105.3±63.3 to 84.2±46.6 seconds (p=0.012), and part B decreased from 280.1±139.9 to 212.8±59.7 seconds (p=0.038).
  • Neuropsychiatric Inventory score decreased from 9.8±14.7 to 4.5±8.8 (p=0.006), while MMSE, Attention Questionnaire Scale and Korean Quality of Life did not change significantly.

What changed

A September 29 prospective report provides the first small repeated-protocol feasibility and short-term safety signal for this low-intensity ultrasound approach in amyloid-PET-confirmed early Alzheimer disease.

Strength of evidence

Very low efficacy certainty and preliminary safety evidence from 20 treated participants. The single-arm design, short exposure and follow-up, multiple exploratory outcomes, large baseline variability and lack of sham control preclude causal or durable-benefit inference.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The protocol merits randomized, sham-controlled evaluation but should not change clinical management. The absence of serious events in 20 participants cannot establish uncommon or longer-term safety, and nominal cognitive or behavioral changes may reflect practice, expectation or regression-to-the-mean effects.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to emerging nonpharmacologic therapeutic development and to counseling stakeholders about the difference between feasibility/safety signals and evidence of clinical benefit.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The intervention remains experimental. The study establishes neither authorization nor routine availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did the study show that ultrasound treats Alzheimer disease?
No. Every participant received the intervention, so practice effects, expectation effects and natural variation cannot be separated from treatment effects.
Why is this Clinical Trials rather than Biomarkers?
The central question was an interventional ultrasound protocol. Amyloid PET established eligibility; the study did not evaluate biomarker measurement, interpretation or implementation.
Is the safety evidence sufficient for routine use?
No. Twenty participants and four weeks of treatment can support feasibility but cannot characterize uncommon events, longer-term risk or outcomes outside the study protocol.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Only 20 participants
  • No randomized or sham-control group
  • Four-week treatment period with limited follow-up
  • Multiple exploratory outcomes without evidence of multiplicity control in the abstract
  • No significant change in MMSE, attention or quality of life
  • Insufficient size to estimate uncommon or delayed adverse events

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Park BY, Jo SW, Park TY, et al. Feasibility and safety of repeated low-intensity ultrasound in amyloid PET-positive early Alzheimer's disease: A prospective pilot study. J Alzheimers Dis. Published online September 29, 2026. doi:10.1177/13872877261493067.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials•September 29, 2026

Caregiver psychoeducation meta-analysis finds moderate burden reduction

Across 12 randomized trials, psychoeducational programs combining structured dementia education with skills training reduced informal-caregiver burden versus controls by Hedges' g −0.45 (95% CI −0.61 to −0.28; p<0.001), although the abstract does not report absolute Zarit-score changes, heterogeneity or evidence certainty.

Key quantitative results: Twelve randomized trials were included and meta-analyzed. Psychoeducational interventions reduced caregiver burden versus control conditions with Hedges' g −0.45 (95% CI −0.61 to −0.28; p<0.001).

ManagementCaregiver support

Added September 30, 2026 · DOI:10.1177/07334648261490430; PMID:42811273

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The pooled estimate supports caregiver psychoeducation that pairs disease information with practical skills rather than education alone. The standardized effect is moderate and statistically precise, but the public abstract does not provide total participants, absolute Zarit-score change, intervention intensity, follow-up duration, heterogeneity, risk-of-bias summary or certainty rating. It informs service design but is not a guideline-level mandate.

Study design

The authors conducted a PRISMA 2020 systematic review and REML random-effects meta-analysis of 12 randomized controlled trials. Eligible interventions combined structured dementia education with skills-based training for informal caregivers. Caregiver burden measured by the Zarit Burden Interview or validated adaptations was the primary outcome; comparator type, mean caregiver age and gender composition were examined as moderators.

Key quantitative results

  • Twelve randomized trials were included and meta-analyzed. Psychoeducational interventions reduced caregiver burden versus control conditions with Hedges' g −0.45 (95% CI −0.61 to −0.28; p<0.001).
  • Comparator type was associated with differences in effect estimates, but the authors cautioned that subgroup analyses were exploratory and some categories contained few studies.
  • Mean caregiver age and gender composition were not significant moderators. The abstract did not report an absolute Zarit-score difference, total sample size, heterogeneity statistic or formal certainty-of-evidence rating.

What changed

A September 29 quantitative synthesis consolidates randomized-trial evidence for psychoeducational caregiver programs and estimates a moderate standardized reduction in burden.

Strength of evidence

Moderate pooled randomized evidence for reduced caregiver burden, tempered by incomplete public reporting of sample size, heterogeneity, intervention components, follow-up, risk of bias and certainty. The comparator moderator is exploratory and some subgroups were sparse.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Programs that combine dementia education with skills training are reasonable components of caregiver support and may reduce burden. The standardized effect does not identify a universal format, dose or absolute benefit, and implementation should reflect caregiver needs, language, access and local resources.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to nonpharmacologic dementia management, caregiver intervention design and conversations about evidence-based supportive services beyond medication or biomarker testing.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The review supports psychoeducational caregiver services but establishes no new program availability, payer coverage or reimbursement. Local access, language, staffing and delivery format remain implementation determinants.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
What does Hedges' g −0.45 mean?
It indicates a moderate average reduction in burden on a standardized scale. The abstract does not provide an absolute Zarit-score change, so it cannot be translated directly into points for an individual caregiver.
Is this a clinical practice guideline?
No. It is a systematic review and meta-analysis of trials. It summarizes evidence but does not issue graded recommendations from a guideline body.
Which program should services adopt?
The pooled abstract does not establish one optimal format or dose. Programs should include both structured education and skills training, while selection should account for setting, caregiver needs and feasibility.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Public abstract does not report total participants or absolute Zarit-score changes
  • Intervention content, intensity and follow-up likely varied across trials
  • Heterogeneity and risk-of-bias results are not reported in the abstract
  • No formal certainty-of-evidence rating is reported publicly in the abstract
  • Comparator-type moderator analyses were exploratory with sparse categories
  • A standardized pooled effect does not identify the most effective delivery model

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Martínez-Montás GF, Iniesta-Sepúlveda M, Colón-Santana OR, Moreta-Manzueta GE. Effectiveness of psychoeducational interventions for informal caregivers of people with dementia: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Appl Gerontol. Published online September 29, 2026. doi:10.1177/07334648261490430.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed real-world clinical and analytical performance study•September 28, 2026

Routine LUMIPULSE p-tau217 stayed stable across 18 months

In 744 cognitively impaired Mayo Clinic patients, a laboratory-developed LUMIPULSE plasma p-tau217 workflow classified amyloid pathology with 93% accuracy among definite results; 23% were intermediate, while quality-control imprecision was 5%–8% and lot-to-lot bias remained within 11% over 18 months.

Key quantitative results: Of 744 patients, 500 (67%) were amyloid-positive. Plasma p-tau217 results were positive in 421 (57%), intermediate in 169 (23%) and negative in 154 (21%). Excluding intermediate results, sensitivity was 98% (95% CI 95%–99%), specificity 84% (77%–89%), PPV 92% (90%–95%), NPV 94% (90%–97%) and accuracy 93% (91%–95%).

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217AmyloidBiological confirmation

Added September 30, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/alz.71887; PMID:42805946; PMCID:PMC13619724

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This is unusually useful post-implementation evidence because it joins clinical validity to longitudinal analytical surveillance rather than reporting a one-time research-cohort AUC. Definite results were accurate in a tertiary specialty population, but nearly one quarter were intermediate and renal impairment shifted more amyloid-negative patients into that category. Stable quality control and reagent comparisons support robustness of the local LDT; they do not validate every laboratory workflow or prove decision impact.

Study design

Investigators evaluated 744 unique Mayo Clinic patients with cognitive impairment seen from July 2024 through December 2025 at campuses in Minnesota, Florida and Arizona. Amyloid status was determined by florbetapir PET and/or CSF p-tau181/Aβ42 within one year of blood collection. Standalone plasma p-tau217 was measured on LUMIPULSE G1200 using pre-established negative, intermediate and positive cutpoints. Analytical monitoring spanned 18 months, 10 reagent lots, two reagent versions, twice-daily quality controls and a 187-sample version comparison.

Key quantitative results

  • Of 744 patients, 500 (67%) were amyloid-positive. Plasma p-tau217 results were positive in 421 (57%), intermediate in 169 (23%) and negative in 154 (21%). Excluding intermediate results, sensitivity was 98% (95% CI 95%–99%), specificity 84% (77%–89%), PPV 92% (90%–95%), NPV 94% (90%–97%) and accuracy 93% (91%–95%).
  • Against amyloid PET alone, sensitivity was 99% and specificity 69%; against CSF p-tau181/Aβ42, sensitivity was 95% and specificity 85%. PET and CSF themselves had 87% overall agreement among 76 patients tested with both methods.
  • Manufacturer-control imprecision was 5%–8%; an in-house pool near the negative cutpoint showed 12%–14% CV. Ten lot comparisons had R² above 0.990 and bias from ±2% to 11%; the reagent-version comparison (n=187) showed R² 0.99 and mean bias −4.35%. Reduced eGFR was associated with more intermediate results among amyloid-negative patients (adjusted p=0.008 for eGFR <45 versus at least 60 mL/min/1.73 m²).

What changed

A September 28 publication supplies 18-month, routine-practice evidence linking clinical classification performance with quality control, reagent-lot and assay-version surveillance for a standalone LUMIPULSE p-tau217 laboratory-developed test.

Strength of evidence

Strong implementation-oriented analytical robustness evidence from routine testing and pre-established cutpoints, with moderate clinical-validity evidence. Interpretation is limited by tertiary-specialty prevalence, two nonidentical reference standards, exclusion of intermediate results from accuracy estimates, few patients with severe renal impairment and a local LDT workflow that is not the FDA-cleared ratio product.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings support sustained laboratory performance of this specific local workflow and reinforce the value of two-cutpoint interpretation and ongoing lot surveillance. A 23% intermediate rate and renal-function effects remain operationally important, and no patient-outcome or decision-impact benefit was tested.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to blood-biomarker implementation, cutpoint governance, quality assurance, renal-function interpretation and communication about the distinction between an LDT and an FDA-cleared assay.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The clinical workflow used a Mayo Clinic laboratory-developed standalone p-tau217 test with pre-established local cutpoints on the LUMIPULSE G1200. It is not the FDA-cleared Fujirebio pTau217/Aβ42 plasma ratio and should not inherit that product's labeled intended use.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, commercial-availability, guideline or coverage change occurred. The report concerns a Mayo Clinic LDT; laboratories adopting any workflow still need product- and matrix-specific validation, quality control and appropriate interpretation processes.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was this the FDA-cleared LUMIPULSE plasma ratio?
No. The study used standalone LUMIPULSE p-tau217 with Mayo Clinic LDT cutpoints. The cleared Fujirebio product measures the pTau217/Aβ42 ratio under a different labeled intended use.
Does 93% accuracy include intermediate results?
No. Intermediate results, which occurred in 23% of patients, were excluded from sensitivity, specificity and accuracy calculations and require further evaluation.
Did the study establish clinical utility?
Not directly. It supports analytical robustness and clinical validity, but it did not test whether the workflow improves decisions, time to diagnosis, treatment access, safety, cost or patient outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective tertiary-center population with 67% amyloid prevalence
  • Mixed amyloid PET and CSF reference standards with only 87% agreement in paired cases
  • Intermediate results excluded from accuracy estimates despite comprising 23% of the cohort
  • Only 23 patients had eGFR below 45 mL/min/1.73 m²
  • Local LDT cutpoints and workflows may not transfer to other laboratories or products
  • No prospective decision-impact, health-economic, treatment-access or patient-outcome evaluation

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record · Free full text

Ashrafzadeh-Kian S, Figdore DJ, Bornhorst JA, et al. Long term clinical performance and analytical robustness of the Lumipulse plasma p-tau217 assay in routine clinical practice. Alzheimers Dement. 2026;22(10):e71887. doi:10.1002/alz.71887.

Early signal•Peer-reviewed retrospective development and independent hold-out validation study•September 27, 2026

Local LLM reaches expert-level lecanemab pre-screen accuracy

In a 99-record independent hold-out set, an on-premises language-model pipeline classified lecanemab eligibility with 93.9% accuracy and κ 0.903, outperforming a deterministic rule-based extractor (79.8% accuracy; p=0.0026), but it remains an uncertified single-center retrospective triage tool requiring clinician review.

Key quantitative results: In the 99-record hold-out set, consensus classified 16 as eligible, 43 as potentially eligible and 40 as not eligible. The LLM pipeline achieved 93.9% accuracy (95% CI 88.9% to 98.0%) and κ 0.903 (95% CI 0.810 to 0.968), with six disagreements.

ManagementDisease-modifying treatment eligibility

Added September 28, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/dad2.70495; PMID:42802831

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The privacy-preserving pipeline could reduce chart-review burden and flag missing amyloid, MRI or cognitive data without sending protected health information to an external cloud. Its hold-out performance was comparable to two expert raters, but six errors included medication/disease categorization, context interpretation and threshold application. Prospective multicenter validation is needed before operational deployment.

Study design

The investigators used 97 German memory-clinic consultation reports to optimize prompts, a deterministic comparator and a shared three-class eligibility rule set, then locked the systems before evaluating 99 temporally and patient-wise distinct hold-out reports. Two clinicians independently classified the hold-out set as eligible, potentially eligible or not eligible, with consensus as the reference standard.

Key quantitative results

  • In the 99-record hold-out set, consensus classified 16 as eligible, 43 as potentially eligible and 40 as not eligible. The LLM pipeline achieved 93.9% accuracy (95% CI 88.9% to 98.0%) and κ 0.903 (95% CI 0.810 to 0.968), with six disagreements.
  • For case finding after combining eligible and potentially eligible, sensitivity was 91.5% (95% CI 83.1% to 98.3%) and specificity 97.5% (95% CI 91.1% to 100.0%); PPV was 98%. Eligible-class sensitivity was 100%.
  • The deterministic extractor achieved 79.8% accuracy and κ 0.673. The paired accuracy difference was 14.1 percentage points (95% CI 6.1 to 22.2; McNemar p=0.0026), while individual experts achieved 91.9% and 93.9% accuracy.

What changed

A September 27 publication now provides locked hold-out performance for a locally deployed language model intended to support lecanemab eligibility pre-screening while keeping patient records on premises.

Strength of evidence

Promising but early implementation evidence with strict separation of development and hold-out sets, a consensus reference and paired comparator. Generalizability is limited by retrospective single-center German documentation, only 99 validation records, local AUR-derived rules, missing APOE information and no prospective workflow, patient-safety or access outcome.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The system may help triage charts and identify missing workup elements, but it should not determine eligibility or replace clinician review. Eligibility remains governed by the applicable label, clinical evaluation, amyloid confirmation, MRI findings, comorbidities, concomitant medications and shared decision-making.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to operational scaling of disease-modifying therapy programs, protected-data handling, chart abstraction and consistency of eligibility review. It is management workflow research, not biomarker-validation evidence.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The model extracted eligibility-relevant facts from German narrative memory-clinic reports and fed them to a shared rule-based classifier. Performance depends on local documentation, operationalized criteria and human oversight; the model was not tested as an autonomous decision-maker.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The on-premises design addresses data-protection barriers and may improve screening capacity, but no commercial availability, medical-device authorization, reimbursement or coverage was established.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was the model tested prospectively in routine care?
No. The study retrospectively classified narrative reports; it did not measure clinician time, missed contraindications in live use, treatment access, safety or patient outcomes.
Why is this not tagged Biomarkers?
Its central question was automated treatment-eligibility triage. Amyloid and MRI information were input variables, not the object of biomarker measurement, validity or interpretation research.
Can the model make treatment decisions?
No. It is an uncertified triage support system, made six hold-out errors and cannot infer facts absent from the record; the authors call for clinician supervision and prospective validation.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center study using German consultation reports
  • Small 99-record independent validation set with only 16 fully eligible cases
  • Local AUR-derived rules may not match labels or policies in other jurisdictions
  • APOE genotype was missing and source documentation predated routine anti-amyloid implementation
  • Six validation errors included medication, disease, context and threshold interpretation
  • No prospective time-saving, decision-impact, safety, access or patient-outcome evaluation

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record · Free full text

Miklitz C, Shrestha M, Philipp W, et al. Locally deployed large language model for real-world lecanemab eligibility pre-screening. Alzheimers Dement (Amst). 2026;18(3):e70495. doi:10.1002/dad2.70495.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed real-world diagnostic-accuracy cohort•September 24, 2026

Standalone LUMIPULSE p-tau217 exceeds 90/90 in treatment candidates

In 99 Japanese patients undergoing anti-amyloid-treatment screening, standalone LUMIPULSE plasma p-tau217 identified PET- or CSF-confirmed amyloid positivity with AUC 0.93, 95.1% sensitivity and 94.1% specificity at a cohort-derived 0.1795 pg/mL cutpoint, but the 80.0% negative predictive value and threshold instability argue against using a negative result alone to exclude treatment candidacy.

Key quantitative results: Amyloid positivity was confirmed in 82/99 (82.8%). Plasma p-tau217 achieved AUC 0.93 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.00); at 0.1795 pg/mL there were 78 true positives, 16 true negatives, one false positive and four false negatives, yielding 95.1% sensitivity, 94.1% specificity, 98.7% PPV and 80.0% NPV.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217AmyloidBiological confirmation

Added September 28, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/dad2.70497; PMID:42787809

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The cohort addresses the exact high-prevalence population in which blood tests may be used to streamline confirmatory testing before anti-amyloid therapy. Performance met the Alzheimer’s Association 90% sensitivity/specificity benchmark at an internally selected threshold, but only 17 patients were amyloid-negative, three of four false negatives were below the assay detection limit, and external higher cutpoints reduced NPV to 55.2%. This is clinical-validity and workflow evidence, not analytical validation or proof that blood-first triage improves outcomes.

Study design

Investigators studied 99 patients evaluated for amyloid-targeting treatment at one Japanese specialty clinic from January through October 2024: 62 had MCI and 37 mild dementia. Amyloid status was confirmed by approved CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 testing in 49 or amyloid PET in 50. Stored plasma was batch-tested for p-tau217 on LUMIPULSE G1200; diagnostic performance was assessed against the PET/CSF reference standard, with the main cutpoint selected in the same cohort by the Youden index.

Key quantitative results

  • Amyloid positivity was confirmed in 82/99 (82.8%). Plasma p-tau217 achieved AUC 0.93 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.00); at 0.1795 pg/mL there were 78 true positives, 16 true negatives, one false positive and four false negatives, yielding 95.1% sensitivity, 94.1% specificity, 98.7% PPV and 80.0% NPV.
  • Three external LUMIPULSE p-tau217 cutpoints from 0.212 to 0.247 pg/mL preserved 94.1% specificity and PPV above 98% but lowered sensitivity to 84.1%–90.2% and NPV as low as 55.2%.
  • A two-cutpoint strategy using 0.1465 pg/mL for negativity and 0.1795 pg/mL for positivity classified 5.1% as intermediate and produced 97.5% sensitivity, 92.9% specificity, 98.7% PPV and 86.7% NPV; the authors still advised confirmatory testing after a negative result when pretest probability is high.

What changed

A newly indexed, source-date September 24 study provides real-world performance data for standalone automated p-tau217 specifically among patients already screened as potential candidates for amyloid-targeting treatment.

Strength of evidence

Moderate clinical-validity evidence from a clinically relevant cohort with PET or approved CSF reference testing. Confidence is limited by the single-center retrospective design, only 17 amyloid-negative participants, selection and biobank-enrollment bias, batch testing, internally optimized threshold and no independent validation cohort.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A positive result was highly predictive in this enriched cohort, but negative results were not sufficiently reliable to rule out amyloid pathology. The data support locally validated triage workflows and prevalence-aware interpretation, not substitution of this standalone research cutpoint for labeled assays or confirmatory testing without further validation.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to blood-based biomarker implementation, anti-amyloid treatment workup, threshold transferability and communication about why PPV/NPV change with population prevalence.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Stored plasma was batch-tested on the LUMIPULSE G1200. The study evaluated standalone p-tau217 with a locally optimized cutpoint, not the FDA-cleared LUMIPULSE pTau217/Aβ42 plasma ratio and not routine on-demand analytical performance.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The report establishes no new authorization, commercial availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement. Standalone LUMIPULSE plasma p-tau217 was described by the manufacturer as research use only in the United States; the FDA-cleared Fujirebio plasma product is the pTau217/Aβ42 ratio.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did the study validate the FDA-cleared LUMIPULSE plasma ratio?
No. It evaluated standalone plasma p-tau217 on the LUMIPULSE platform. The US-cleared Fujirebio test uses the pTau217/Aβ42 ratio with its labeled interpretation.
Can a negative result rule out amyloid pathology before treatment?
Not reliably in this high-prevalence cohort. NPV was 80.0% at the optimized single cutpoint and 86.7% with two cutpoints; the authors advised confirmatory testing when clinical suspicion remains high.
Was clinical utility proven?
No. The study measured diagnostic classification in stored samples; it did not test whether a blood-first strategy changes treatment decisions, time to care, cost, safety or patient outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Single specialty center in Japan with only 99 participants and 17 amyloid-negative cases
  • Very high amyloid prevalence and biobank-enrollment bias inflate PPV and constrain NPV precision
  • Primary threshold selected and evaluated in the same cohort without external validation
  • Batch testing of stored plasma may understate routine on-demand variability
  • Mixed PET and CSF reference standards and incomplete APOE data
  • No analytical-validation, decision-impact, health-economic or patient-outcome endpoint

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record · Free full text

Shimasaki R, Kurihara M, Sato K, et al. Clinical utility of LUMIPULSE plasma p-tau217 to identify amyloid positivity among candidates for amyloid-targeting treatments in a real-world cohort. Alzheimers Dement (Amst). 2026;18(3):e70497. doi:10.1002/dad2.70497.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective real-world treatment cohort•September 24, 2026

Japanese lecanemab cohort quantifies screening and early ARIA

Of 321 patients screened at one Japanese memory clinic, 102 started lecanemab; among 70 with serial MRI surveillance, 8 (11.4%) developed ARIA within six months, while infusion reactions occurred in 28/102 (27.5%) and 13/102 (12.7%) discontinued treatment.

Key quantitative results: Treatment started in 102/321 (31.8%). Before amyloid testing, 154/320 (48.1%) were excluded or deferred after MRI/cognitive assessment; 54/165 (32.5%) who underwent amyloid PET were negative, and 13/102 (12.7%) treated patients discontinued within six months.

ManagementMRIDisease-modifying treatment eligibility

Added September 28, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/dad2.70492; PMID:42798750

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This cohort exposes the operational funnel around lecanemab: only 31.8% of clinically suspected patients initiated treatment after cognition, MRI, amyloid confirmation and preference were considered. Early safety was broadly manageable under structured MRI surveillance, but four ARIA cases led to discontinuation and nearly one in eight treated patients stopped for clinical, logistical or financial reasons. The uncontrolled six-month cognitive data cannot establish effectiveness.

Study design

A Japanese memory clinic retrospectively followed 321 people with suspected MCI due to Alzheimer disease or mild Alzheimer dementia considered for lecanemab. MRI and structured cognitive testing preceded amyloid confirmation; 102 patients received at least one infusion. Safety and continuity analyses included all treated patients, ARIA incidence used the 70 who had serial MRI surveillance within six months, and paired cognitive analyses included 66 six-month completers.

Key quantitative results

  • Treatment started in 102/321 (31.8%). Before amyloid testing, 154/320 (48.1%) were excluded or deferred after MRI/cognitive assessment; 54/165 (32.5%) who underwent amyloid PET were negative, and 13/102 (12.7%) treated patients discontinued within six months.
  • ARIA occurred in 8/70 (11.4%) patients with serial MRI: isolated ARIA-H in 10.0% and combined ARIA-E+H in 1.4%, with no isolated ARIA-E. One macrohemorrhage and two moderate-to-severe ARIA-H cases led to discontinuation; a fourth mild ARIA-H case stopped because of advanced age.
  • Infusion reactions occurred in 28/102 (27.5%), most commonly fever (14.7%); 2/102 (2.0%) discontinued for persistent reactions. Among 66 six-month completers, MMSE fell from 25.0 to 23.9 (p=0.005) and CDR-SB rose from 1.56 to 1.77 (p=0.026), without an untreated comparator.

What changed

A newly indexed, source-date September 24 cohort provides a complete real-world screening funnel plus structured six-month ARIA, infusion-reaction, persistence and discontinuation data from routine Japanese practice.

Strength of evidence

Moderate implementation and safety evidence from a well-described real-world cohort with structured MRI surveillance. The single-center retrospective design, changing denominators, short follow-up, mild treated population and absence of a control group prevent causal efficacy comparisons or precise risk estimates for broader practice.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The study reinforces the need to plan MRI capacity, infusion-reaction management and counseling about treatment burden before initiation. Its ARIA estimates should not replace label-based monitoring or individualized risk assessment, and the six-month cognitive changes should not be interpreted as proof of benefit or failure.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to disease-modifying treatment eligibility, operational access, ARIA surveillance, APOE discussions, infusion management and persistence in routine care.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Lecanemab was covered by Japanese national insurance, but copayments of 10%–30%, frequent infusions and travel affected uptake or persistence. The study documents access friction; it does not establish a new coverage or reimbursement policy.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
How many screened patients actually started lecanemab?
102 of 321 (31.8%). Cognitive stage, MRI safety findings, amyloid negativity, patient preference and logistical or financial concerns all narrowed the funnel.
Was the ARIA rate 11.4% of all 102 treated patients?
No. The numerator was eight and the denominator was 70 patients with serial MRI surveillance within six months. The publication used changing denominators as patients reached follow-up milestones.
Did stable six-month cognition demonstrate effectiveness?
No. Only 66 completers had paired measures, MMSE and CDR-SB worsened modestly, and there was no untreated comparator.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center cohort with modest treated sample
  • ARIA estimate based on 70 serially monitored patients rather than all 102 treated patients
  • Only six months of follow-up and predominantly CDR 0.5 disease
  • No untreated or matched comparator for cognitive outcomes
  • Selection, treatment-preference and attrition effects limit generalizability
  • Japanese eligibility, reimbursement and MRI practice may differ from other jurisdictions

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record · Free full text

Shimohama S, Bun S, Shikimoto R, et al. Real-world implementation of lecanemab in Alzheimer's disease: A Japanese cohort. Alzheimers Dement (Amst). 2026;18(3):e70492. doi:10.1002/dad2.70492.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed consecutive real-world memory-clinic biomarker cohort•September 23, 2026

Real-world amyloid PET yield rises across the clinical continuum

In 194 consecutive memory-clinic patients, amyloid PET positivity rose from 40.9% in subjective cognitive decline to 66.0% in MCI and 91.7% in early Alzheimer disease, while MRI/VSRAD indices added essentially no discrimination beyond clinical diagnosis (cross-validated AUC 0.752 versus 0.751).

Key quantitative results: Amyloid PET positivity increased stepwise from 38/93 (40.9%) in subjective cognitive decline to 31/47 (66.0%) in MCI and 50/54 (91.7%) in early Alzheimer disease (p<0.0001).

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloidBiological confirmation

Added September 24, 2026 · DOI:10.1177/13872877261490596; PMID:42775784

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The consecutive-clinic design gives useful real-world context for pretest probability and shows that commonly used structural MRI indices did not add amyloid-status discrimination. It supports clinical validity of amyloid PET in the studied setting, not analytical validation or clinical utility: no management-change or outcome endpoint was tested, and positivity in subjective cognitive decline should not be equated with a clinical Alzheimer diagnosis.

Study design

The investigators retrospectively analyzed 194 consecutive patients who underwent florbetapir PET in one memory-clinic setting: 93 with subjective cognitive decline, 47 with MCI and 54 with early Alzheimer disease. Certified visual reads defined positivity; continuous Centiloid and regional SUVR measures quantified burden. MRI/VSRAD indices were available for 153 patients, and models were compared with cross-validated AUC.

Key quantitative results

  • Amyloid PET positivity increased stepwise from 38/93 (40.9%) in subjective cognitive decline to 31/47 (66.0%) in MCI and 50/54 (91.7%) in early Alzheimer disease (p<0.0001).
  • Centiloid values and regional SUVRs increased in parallel across the groups, with the largest regional differences in the temporal cortex and precuneus.
  • Adding MRI/VSRAD indices to the base clinical model did not improve cross-validated discrimination of amyloid positivity: AUC 0.752 with MRI versus 0.751 without it.

What changed

A source-date-new consecutive memory-clinic study now quantifies amyloid PET positivity across subjective cognitive decline, MCI and early Alzheimer disease and directly tests the incremental value of routinely used MRI/VSRAD indices.

Strength of evidence

Moderate real-world clinical-validity evidence from a consecutive cohort with certified reads and cross-validation. The single-center retrospective design, clinically assigned groups, incomplete MRI data and absence of a decision-impact or patient-outcome endpoint limit implementation claims.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The observed gradient can inform pretest-probability discussions, and the near-identical AUCs argue against assuming that VSRAD meaningfully predicts amyloid status beyond clinical classification. PET results still require interpretation in the full clinical context and according to the tracer label.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to amyloid-confirmation pathways, DMT workup discussions and the distinction between structural neurodegeneration markers and amyloid pathology. It also illustrates why a positive scan is not itself a stand-alone clinical diagnosis.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Amyloid status was assigned by certified visual reads and quantified with Centiloids and regional SUVRs. VSRAD MRI indices correlated with amyloid burden but did not improve cross-validated discrimination beyond the clinical group model.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No new authorization, tracer availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from this report.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does 40.9% positivity in subjective cognitive decline support screening asymptomatic people?
No. This was a referred memory-clinic cohort, not a population-screening sample, and the study did not test benefits, harms or outcomes from screening.
Did MRI add useful prediction of amyloid positivity?
Not in the cross-validated models: the AUC changed from 0.751 to 0.752 after VSRAD indices were added.
Was clinical utility established?
No. The study measured biomarker prevalence and discrimination; it did not test whether PET-guided decisions changed management or improved outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Single-center retrospective cohort with a modest sample
  • Memory-clinic referral population limits generalizability and cannot estimate population screening yield
  • MRI/VSRAD data were available for 153 of 194 participants
  • Clinical categories were not an independent neuropathology reference standard
  • No management-change, decision-impact, cost-effectiveness or patient-outcome endpoint

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Arai H, Aiba S, Yamamoto H, Akiba Y, Takayama J, Arai R. Clinic-based real-world analysis of amyloid PET positivity and MRI markers across subjective cognitive decline, mild cognitive impairment, and early Alzheimer's disease. J Alzheimers Dis. Published online September 23, 2026. doi:10.1177/13872877261490596.

Sponsor-reported phase 2 findings support further study of diranersen; they do not establish treatment benefit.

Clinical TrialsManagementCSFTotal tauTau PETDisease-modifying treatment

Added September 7, 2026 · NCT05399888

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The primary endpoint failed, and favorable secondary comparisons require confirmation.

Study design

CELIA randomized 416 anti-amyloid-naive participants with MCI or mild AD dementia to intrathecal diranersen or placebo for 18 months.

Key quantitative results

  • At 60 mg every 6 months (n=60) versus placebo (n=115), the reported CDR-SB difference was −0.54 points, or 26% less decline. Confidence intervals were not supplied in the cited release.
  • The 115 mg regimens showed smaller CDR-SB differences (−0.28 and −0.18); ADCS-ADL-MCI did not separate from placebo.

What changed

July data quantify the earlier topline announcement.

Strength of evidence

Randomized design, but conference/sponsor reporting with a failed primary endpoint.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Insufficient for clinical use.

Field medical relevance

Keep nominal secondary findings separate from confirmatory evidence.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Tau reduction does not establish an assay’s clinical utility.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No approval, availability or coverage claim.

Lecanemab labeling adds subcutaneous treatment initiation

The July label permits weekly subcutaneous initiation, extending home-injection options beyond maintenance treatment.

Key label details: Subcutaneous starting dose is 500 mg weekly, as two 250 mg injections. After 18 months, continuing that regimen or transitioning to maintenance is permitted.

ManagementDisease-modifying treatment

Added September 7, 2026 · BLA 761375/S-001; FDA label reference 5833017

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Route convenience changes delivery planning, while amyloid confirmation, early symptomatic eligibility and ARIA precautions remain.

Study design

Label update for initiation in MCI or mild AD dementia, with confirmed amyloid pathology.

Key label details

  • Subcutaneous starting dose is 500 mg weekly, as two 250 mg injections. After 18 months, continuing that regimen or transitioning to maintenance is permitted.
  • Subcutaneous maintenance is 360 mg weekly. The label specifies baseline MRI and monitoring after 1, 2, 3 and 6 months.

What changed

Subcutaneous dosing can begin at treatment initiation.

Strength of evidence

Authoritative dosing instructions; not a new head-to-head clinical-benefit trial.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Initiation and maintenance strengths must remain distinct.

Field medical relevance

Discuss delivery burden together with safety infrastructure.

Access or reimbursement relevance

FDA authorization is verified. Current supply, coverage and patient cost are not established here.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does home dosing remove ARIA monitoring?
No. The boxed warning and MRI surveillance still apply.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • This route change does not establish superior cognition outcomes or lower ARIA risk.
  • APOE ε4 homozygotes face higher ARIA risk; consult genotype counseling and risk instructions.
